definition: Complicit means involved as a knowing partner in wrongdoing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word complicit. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know complicit should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The timekeeper who logged twelve-hour shifts as eight was complicit in the mill's scheme to cheat its weavers of overtime.
Someone wholly unaware of a scheme cannot share its guilt; unaware sits at the bottom of the ladder and stops far short of complicit.
To be aware of wrongdoing and stay silent is troubling, but aware stops short of complicit, which requires playing a knowing part.

Involved says only that you were caught up in the affair — possibly innocently, possibly without understanding a thing. Complicit adds the two elements that convict: knowing the scheme was wrong, and playing a knowing part in it anyway. Every complicit person is involved; the reverse is not true.

Cooperating means working together toward a shared aim, and it carries no shade of crime — nurses cooperate, allies cooperate, rescue crews cooperate. Complicit is cooperation gone criminal: a knowing partnership in wrongdoing. Call people cooperating and you praise their teamwork; call them complicit and you accuse them.

The diamond appraiser insisted he had merely valued the stones brought to him; but he had valued the same stolen stones five times under five different names, and the court held him complicit in the fencing ring.
Complicit is precise about two things at once: participation and knowledge.
A courier who unknowingly carries stolen goods is involved but not complicit — the word requires that you understood the wrong and lent yourself to it anyway.
Complicit describes what you are; abet (also in this unit) names what you do.
A silent witness is sometimes called complicit in a loose, accusing way, but strictly the word wants both knowledge and a part played — save it for the partner, not the bystander.

When the celebrated coral-reef study collapsed, attention fixed first on the postdoc who had typed the fabricated numbers into the spreadsheets.
But the university's inquiry drew a wider circle.

A lab manager had reordered reagents for experiments she knew had never been run, and a co-author had signed off on figures after privately noting they were 'too clean to be real.' The inquiry called both of them complicit: neither had invented a single data point, yet each had lent knowing help to the deception.
Only the department's grant clerk walked away clear -- she had processed the paperwork, the report concluded, with no way of knowing what lay behind it.
